Fortreum Launches Kovr-Powered VDR/VER Offering Ahead of FedRAMP Vulnerability Deadline

📅 Nov 13, 2026  |  Category: Technology  |  Read Source →

Fortreum has introduced its Kovr-powered VDR/VER offering to help cloud providers put FedRAMP’s new vulnerability rules into operation ahead of the December 7, 2026 migration deadline. The offering combines security specialists, implementation support, and AI-assisted evaluation rather than treating compliance as a scanner report that gets filed once a month.

In its technical explanation, Fortreum describes a workflow that connects scan findings to assets, produces first-pass vulnerability evaluations, and tracks response activity and evidence. Customer teams review the determinations and direct the response.

The distinction matters because identifying a software flaw is only the beginning. A provider also needs to establish where it exists, whether an attacker can reach it, what exploitation would affect, and why its response is appropriate.

FedRAMP is the U.S. government’s program for assessing and overseeing the security of cloud services used by federal agencies. Its updated vulnerability rules split the work into two closely related areas.

Vulnerability Detection and Response, or VDR, covers identifying and managing vulnerabilities over time. Vulnerability Evaluation and Reporting, or VER, concerns evaluating their implications and reporting the relevant information.

A severity score alone cannot answer every operational question. The same flaw could appear on an isolated test machine and on a public-facing service holding sensitive information. The software weakness may be identical, while the paths an attacker could take and the consequences of exploitation are very different.

The rules therefore make context important: likely exploitability, internet reachability, potential agency impact, and the effectiveness of mitigation. Providers need to retain the evidence behind those judgments as conditions change.

Fortreum says its implementation approach starts with the provider’s environment and existing vulnerability process, then establishes responsibilities and reporting workflows. Kovr ingests scan and inventory information, associates findings with assets, and prepares initial evaluations of exploitability, reachability, and potential agency impact.

The useful output is more than another list of vulnerabilities. A finding needs an owner, a response deadline, supporting evidence, and a record of what happened next. Keeping those elements connected makes it easier for security engineering and compliance teams to work from the same facts.

For example, an analyst might determine that a vulnerable component is present but not exposed through the service’s external interface. That conclusion needs evidence about the affected asset and its configuration. If a deployment later changes the exposure, the earlier determination may no longer describe the risk.

AI can help organize the records and prepare an evaluation, but the decision remains tied to the provider’s environment. Fortreum explicitly places review and response direction with the customer, rather than presenting automated output as a substitute for the provider’s obligations.

Kovr is Fortreum’s AI-native compliance automation platform for regulated organizations. Its wider capabilities include evidence collection, documentation management, control mapping, remediation tracking, and continuous monitoring support across multiple frameworks.

The platform uses large language models and is built on the Open Security Controls Assessment Language, or OSCAL. OSCAL provides structured formats for exchanging security-control and assessment information between systems. That is different from simply storing a folder of PDFs: structured records can be processed, compared, and reused by software.

Kovr also provides Agent Artemis, a compliance-focused assistant for navigating requirements, locating documentation, and understanding controls. Those capabilities illustrate the surrounding platform; Fortreum’s VDR/VER description focuses specifically on the vulnerability evaluation and response workflow.

Unite.AI previously covered Fortreum’s acquisition of Kovr.AI. The new offering applies that combination of assessment expertise and automation to a concrete operational change in federal cloud oversight.

The deadline needs to be read alongside FedRAMP’s current guidance. In its November 10 migration notice, FedRAMP confirms December 7, 2026 as the migration date and retains a grace period through March 7, 2027 for certified cloud services.

Services that are not fully migrated on December 7 must explain corrective actions and target timelines for each outstanding rule. Those planning to finish after February 3 will be listed as in remediation until completion. FedRAMP also describes case-by-case extensions beyond March 7, requiring an approved corrective action plan and agreement to a coordinated red-team assessment.

Consequently, December 7 is not an automatic certification revocation date for every provider with unfinished work. It is a milestone that requires an operational response and a defensible account of remaining gaps. The notice also calls for migration progress reporting, including example machine-readable and human-readable vulnerability activity reports.

The central challenge is coordinating a continuing process. A scan can reveal a flaw, but reducing its risk may involve an engineer applying a patch, an infrastructure team changing access, and a compliance team recording why the chosen response meets the applicable requirements.

Fortreum’s proposition is to connect that work through a shared dataset and repeatable workflow. The practical measure of success will be whether teams can make timely, well-supported decisions and show the evidence behind them, rather than merely produce more compliance documents.

Microsoft is making progress in resolving the massive global outage that started Thursday morning and affected Microsoft 365, Copilot, and Outlook access in 74 countries, according to Downdetector. But on Friday afternoon, the company said it wasn’t sure when the issue would be fully fixed.

“As infrastructure stabilizes, we’re still draining queued messages and rebalancing traffic, so customers may see improved sign-in/access while delivery and processing continue to catch up,” Microsoft posted in its now long-running X thread about the outage. “We do not have an ETA for full recovery yet. For some frustrated X users in the comments, that might not be enough. While many users are back in Outlook and Teams, the outage has now been affecting some for over 24 hours. On Friday morning, Microsoft shared an update on X that it was “seeing encouraging recovery progress” and that “a growing portion” of Microsoft 365 services was improving, noting in a follow-up post that it was seeing “broader improvements in North America, sustained improvements across much of Europe, and encouraging recovery signals in Asia Pacific.”

Downdetector reports have stayed low as of Friday midday at around 3,000.

“Some users may still experience intermittent issues as recovery actions continue,” Microsoft said. “We’re focused on recovery for the remaining affected environments while prioritizing email queue and backlog reduction. Microsoft has not publicly identified the cause of the outage, but is maintaining it’s not security-related.

Also: Microsoft fixes over 1,000 Windows flaws – and one is being exploited

Charles Lamanna, Microsoft’s executive vice president of Copilot, Agents, and Platform, said on X late Thursday night, “I can confirm that there is no indication this is the result of malicious or cyber activity.”

Microsoft reiterated that late Friday morning in an update to its X thread on the outage.

“We will continue to share more information as we have it, and for now we can confirm that there is no indication this is the result of malicious or cyber activity. Our teams are reviewing what happened and how we can prevent similar issues going forward,” Microsoft wrote.

According to CNN, Microsoft told Australia’s Home Affairs Minister Tony Burke that they “don’t believe they are dealing with a cyber attack.” During a press conference, Burke said Microsoft told him “they believe they are dealing in some ways similar to what we saw with respect to CrowdStrike where there is an update that has gone awry.”

That refers to the great CrowdStrike meltdown of July 2024, in which a software issue disrupted operations at hospitals, airlines, and other major information hubs.

On Thursday morning, multiple people began reporting issues with Outlook, Teams, and Copilot, according to Downdetector. By 1 p.m. ET, the number of reported Outlook outages was nearly 83,000 but had fallen to just under 75,000 by 2:38 p.m. ET. Teams and Copilot reports started dropping significantly by Thursday evening, but many individuals were still reporting issues accessing systems well into Friday morning on X and Reddit. Even Microsoft’s status page was down until around 3 p.m. ET Thursday.

Apartment rents diverge: San Francisco rises, the Sun Belt falls

📅 Nov 13, 2026  |  Category: Technology  |  Read Source →

RealPage reported a 1.7% year-over-year rise in October rents nationally, with the Bay Area posting the strongest gains and many Sun Belt and Florida markets still declining. Deliveries and absorption are nearing balance, and occupancy was 95%.  AI Summary

America’s apartment landscape has become a tale of two opposing rent trends. Rents are climbing in the Bay Area and the Midwest, while much of the Sun Belt is still sliding.

National same-store asking rents edged up 1.7% from a year earlier in October, the biggest annual gain since May 2023, apartment industry data firm RealPage reported Nov. 11.

The national figure hides a wide gap. San Francisco rents jumped 14.7%, evidence of why city officials are pressing the supply button to drive housing construction. San Antonio rents dropped 2.6%.

The month-over-month picture illustrates less dramatic change. RealPage showed that rents fell 0.7% in October, the first monthly cut of 2026. The company said the annual gain came less from strong pricing than from weak months dropping out of the calculation, making for stronger year-over-year comparables.

Other trackers show the same upward drift, with different monthly readings. Yardi Matrix reported rents up 0.1% in October, with annual growth of 1.4%, the strongest in more than three years. Apartments.com put annual growth at 1.6%, even as rents slipped 0.15% for the month.

Supply and demand are edging toward balance. RealPage said renters absorbed nearly 304,800 conventional apartments in the year ending in Q3 2026. Developers completed nearly 318,000 units over the same period, almost half the late-2024 peak.

Occupancy eased to 95%, down 20 basis points from September. It is still up 40 basis points this year and 10 basis points above October 2025.

Improving rents haven’t translated into a property buying spree. Camden Property Trust, a large apartment landlord, walked away from two acquisitions and canceled two planned development projects. The Federal Reserve’s rate hike was a main reason, rental economist Jay Parsons wrote on LinkedIn.

Two deals under contract fell through after the hike, Camden CEO Alex Jessett said on the third-quarter earnings call. Camden asked for lower prices, and the sellers declined.

Buying also beat building on cost. Camden bought an asset at about $370,000 a door, while building it would have cost north of $600,000, Jessett said.

Camden’s earnings show an unevenly improving market. Funds from operations, a standard earnings measure for real estate investment trusts, were $1.70 per diluted share in the third quarter. Core funds from operations were $1.71, $0.02 above the company’s guidance midpoint.

“A higher-for-longer rate environment may equate to a lower-for-longer supply environment,” Parsons wrote.

Fewer projects penciling out means fewer new apartment options for renters.

Northern California took the top three spots for rent power among the 50 largest markets, RealPage said. San Francisco rose 14.7%, San Jose 9.5% and Oakland 8.5%. All three are running near 97% occupancy.

Midwest metros fill much of the rest of the top 10. Milwaukee led at 4.2%, followed by Chicago at 3.3%, and Kansas City and Cleveland at 3.1% each. Detroit and St. Louis each gained 2.7% and just missed the cut.

Most Sun Belt and Florida markets continued to decline. The South as a region returned to annual growth, but only by 0.5%.

San Antonio had the deepest decline in rents among big markets at 2.6%. Its occupancy of 92.5% was the lowest of the 50 largest markets. Houston fell 1.8%, followed by drops in Tampa of 1%, Charlotte of 0.9% and Denver of 0.8%.

Several Sun Belt markets have turned the corner, however. Jacksonville rose 2.6%, Raleigh 1.0%, Atlanta 0.8%, Austin and Miami 0.6% each, and Phoenix 0.4%.

NVIDIA Says Permanent CEO Search Remains at Search-Firm Stage

📅 Nov 13, 2026  |  Category: Technology  |  Read Source →

NVIDIA’s board said on November 13, 2026, that it was still selecting a search firm to find a permanent CEO and had not formally engaged any potential candidates, CNBC reported, responding to speculation about Jensen Huang’s successor.

The board said, “Any speculation regarding individual candidates, whether internal or external, is premature.” Its wording addresses formal engagement specifically, leaving a distinction between that stage and any informal approach.

That distinction matters because the Financial Times reported on November 13 that the board had approached Arm CEO Rene Haas, citing people familiar with the matter. Haas joined SoftBank-backed Arm in 2013 after seven years at NVIDIA, where his roles included vice president of the computing-products business.

NVIDIA announced on November 12, 2026 that Huang had resigned as president, CEO and a board member, effective immediately. Colette Kress agreed to serve as interim CEO while retaining her executive vice president and CFO duties until a permanent successor is named. She joined NVIDIA in September 2013 after almost 25 years in technology-finance roles, including at Cisco and Microsoft. The permanent search will consider internal and external candidates, and Harvey C. Jones was appointed as the board’s first-ever chair.

Kress held her first meeting as interim CEO on the afternoon of November 12 with senior executives at NVIDIA’s Santa Clara, California, headquarters, according to a person familiar with the internal details. Her dual responsibilities place the executive overseeing NVIDIA’s finances at the center of the company’s leadership while the board organizes the permanent search.

NVIDIA shares fell more than 2% on November 13, moving the company’s market capitalization below $4 trillion. The move came as investors assessed Huang’s departure and the leadership transition.

Jones said the board expected operations, customer commitments and the product roadmap to continue without interruption under Kress and the leadership team.

Kress separately said NVIDIA would continue advancing its accelerated-computing and AI work, with its focus remaining on customers, partners, developers and shareholders.

Third-quarter fiscal 2027 results remain scheduled for November 17, 2026, at approximately 1:20 p.m. Pacific Time, followed by the earnings call at 2 p.m. Pacific Time. That release is the next scheduled public checkpoint for the continuity plan.

It will come while Kress holds both the interim CEO and CFO roles and the board is still selecting the firm that will support the search. The immediate business issue is therefore whether the existing leadership team can deliver the operational and product-roadmap continuity the board has promised while the permanent succession remains unresolved.

Movement Mortgage seeks to recoup $1.2M from former LOs

📅 Nov 13, 2026  |  Category: Technology  |  Read Source →

Movement Mortgage is moving to enforce an arbitration ruling that says former loan officers Victor Shkolnikov and Igor Velyunskiy must repay $1.235 million in signing bonuses after leaving about a year into their three-year commitments.  AI Summary

Movement Mortgage wants two former loan officers to pay back a total of more than $1.2 million in signing bonuses after they left the company about a year into their three-year agreements.

According to court and arbitration documents, Movement paid a total of $1,235,000 in “start-up payments” to loan officers Victor Shkolnikov and Igor Velyunskiy when they joined the company in March 2022. Shkolnikov received $835,000 and Velyunskiy received $400,000.

The contracts said these payments were advances on future wages and had to be paid back in full if the loan officers left before working 36 consecutive months at the company. If they left early, the money was due within 30 days.

Both Shkolnikov and Velyunskiy left Movement around March 2023, roughly one year into their three-year commitment. Public records show Shkolnikov now works as a loan originator with United Lending Team in Illinois, while Velyunskiy is with Smart Rate Lending LLC.

Movement and the two former loan officers did not immediately respond to HousingWire’s requests for comment. National Mortgage News first reported the dispute.

Movement started arbitration in February 2024, and the cases were combined before arbitrator H. William Constangy. The LOs pushed back, filing counterclaims that accuse Movement of breach of contract, unjust enrichment, fraudulent inducement and violations of the Truth in Lending Act.

In July, the arbitrator ruled in favor of Movement. The decision said the employment agreements were valid contracts and that the two breached the contracts when they did not repay the start-up payments after leaving before the 36-month mark. All of their counterclaims were dismissed.

The award says the repayment amount will also accrue interest at North Carolina’s legal rate of 8% per year, starting in April 2023, which the arbitrator treated as the date of the breach. The arbitrator did not order either side to pay the other’s legal fees, so each party must cover its own attorneys’ costs.

In early November, Movement asked the U.S. District Court for the Western District of North Carolina, Charlotte Division, to confirm the arbitration award and turn it into a court judgment. That would make it easier for the lender to collect the money if it isn’t paid voluntarily.

<a href="https://www.fiercehealthcare.com/health-tech/industry-voices-pledges-progress-kill-clipboard-keep-eye-consistency" hreflang="en">Industry Voices—From pledges to progress: Kill the clipboard, keep an eye on consistency</a>

📅 2026-11-13  |  Category: Technology  |  Read Source →
Industry Voices—From pledges to progress: Kill the clipboard, keep an eye on consistency" style="max-width:100%; height:auto; border-radius:8px;" loading="lazy">

For many patients, the clipboard remains one of healthcare’s most familiar frustrations.

At nearly every visit, patients are asked to provide information they have already supplied elsewhere, including their insurance coverage, medications, family history and previous surgeries. This repetitious hassle—even if managed on tablets as in recent years—frustrates patients, increases the risk of incomplete or inaccurate information entering the record, and takes unnecessary staff time to reconcile.

The Centers for Medicare & Medicaid Services’ Health Technology Ecosystem initiative offers a compelling alternative through the Kill the Clipboard pledge. The effort is focused on moving technology and care practices forward so that patients can more easily retrieve and share their health information through personal health records or other health apps, removing the need for their data to be reconstructed at every encounter.

That shift could conclusively improve the patient experience. Reaching that goal, however, will require more than voluntary commitments from individual technology developers. This multi-stakeholder initiative needs work based on consensus-based standards, reliable infrastructure, clear data governance and careful attention to how new capabilities affect clinical work.

Patients often assume that health data interoperability is happening more than it is, and certainly more easily. In some cases, a person opens an app and shares their information with a provider themselves; in others, the exchange is initiated by their clinical care team. Behind that process, though, is a complex chain of care organizations, electronic health records (EHRs), identity verification services, intermediaries, standards development organizations, application developers and networks.

Consider, for example, real-time prescription benefit information. Giving patients cost and coverage options during an encounter—and ensuring that the information is accurate all the way to the point of sale—could help increase affordability and medication adherence. Yet the experience depends on pharmacy networks, price comparison apps and other third parties delivering complete, timely information into the clinician’s prescribing workflow, all while the patient is there in the exam room or awaiting discharge from the hospital. Every participant in the chain is fundamental to the increasingly complex web of health information exchange.

A 2025 study of more than 8,100 family physicians published in JAMA Network Open underscores just how much work around data-sharing remains. Depending on the type of clinical information, only 8% to 19% of survey respondents reported that outside data were routinely available, easy to find and easy to use within their EHRs.

Pledges like Kill the Clipboard can establish a valuable direction for the industry and encourage momentum. They will face challenges with adoption and impact, however, if sufficient effort doesn’t go into resolving dependencies across the country’s health tech ecosystem. Clear technical standards, realistic implementation timelines and ways to verify that promised capabilities work in practice are essential.

While the goals of increasing patient control over their own data, tackling inefficiencies, and increasing affordable care delivery are laudable and things no one would argue with, it is also true that moving quickly without those foundations could create expensive rework down the road or inadvertently widen the digital divide. If any or all pledge criteria eventually become certification requirements, as Dr. Tom Keane, the National Coordinator for Health IT, has intimated could be a possibility, the variability in readiness among different companies could become a problematic gap.

Expanding digital access also raises important questions about how patient data will be used once it leaves a regulated clinical environment.

There has been a huge proliferation of health apps in recent years intended to help patients more actively manage their own health while also better managing their medical records. Many can deliver meaningful value, but patients who are considering use of such an app need clearer information about whether an application may retain, combine, share or sell their data. Consent language should be understandable, with governance expectations following the information across the digital ecosystem, but the current legal and regulatory system needs modernization to ensure sufficient patient awareness.

Patient matching presents another safety concern. A larger volume of exchanged data is useful only when organizations can confidently connect each record to the correct person. Striking the right balance between the stringency of matching criteria and the goal of increasing data exchange is critical, as a clinician could make a prescribing or treatment decision based on another person’s medications, allergies, diagnoses or laboratory results with damaging consequences. Strong identity verification and thoughtful matching practices therefore belong at the center of any effort to make health data more portable, ensuring that patient safety protections are inherent to the matching process.

The potential consequences have recently been measured. A 2026 BMJ Quality & Safety study found that hospitalized patients with duplicate charts had 3.5 times the odds of requiring intensive care, 4.7 times the odds of inpatient death and hospital stays that were 32% longer than those of matched patients without duplicate charts. Although the observational study does not establish causation, it underscores the clinical risks associated with fragmented patient information.

For virtually any initiative focused on the patient, program vision and software design must also account for the people delivering care.

Primary care clinicians often have only a few minutes to review a patient’s record, conduct their initial assessment of the problem, complete documentation of the encounter, place orders and determine any necessary follow-up. While unquestionably helpful, adding review of new extensive patient data that has been sent from a patient’s medical record aggregation app adds another step that takes time. Then, needing to build in time to consider prescription cost comparisons, scheduling stemming from referrals, discussions of patient consent preferences, or record reconciliation further consumes part of a tightly constrained visit.

The impact on the provider and staff workflows in no way diminishes the value to the patient. These changes benefit all of us as patients and/or caregivers ourselves—but the implications for that workflow cannot be an afterthought.

The strongest implementations will embed new capabilities directly into existing workflows and surface information exactly when it is most useful. Software developers should also involve practicing clinicians in design, testing and governance so that any improvements support better care without introducing avoidable friction. In fact, prioritizing the efficient implementation of these new functionalities will increase adoption and user satisfaction, moving us all closer to our collective goals.

Eliminating the clipboard is the correct ambition, as are the goals of the other Health Tech Ecosystem pledges. They would serve patients nationwide and represent broader industry change in how we move and manage information. Patients should not have to recount their histories every time they seek care, and clinicians should have dependable data available whenever decisions must be made.

With mature standards, real-time connectivity, responsible governance, reliable patient matching and thoughtful workflow design, we can collectively turn the pledge’s aims into a new reality: more trusted digital experiences that give patients greater control and help everyone involved in their care act with greater confidence.

Leigh Burchell is vice president of policy and public affairs at Altera Digital Health, as well as chair of the Electronic Health Record Association.

What's ahead for AI financing after Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang departs

📅 2026-11-13  |  Category: Technology  |  Read Source →

Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang's departure hasn't produced a broad shock to the credit market, but it is putting the company's role as a financier of artificial intelligence infrastructure under scrutiny.

Huang, who stepped down Thursday amid an espionage and adultery scandal, built Nvidia into an AI powerhouse in the 33 years since he co-founded the company. Chief financial officer Colette Kress has been named interim CEO as the company searches for a permanent chief executive.

Nvidia not only supplies its graphics processing units to hyperscalers and tech giants, it also provides financing to other companies to help the industry expand. That could all change.

"Although we expect the company to fulfill all of its previously announced commitments, we believe that going forward, it may be more difficult for the company to negotiate new multi-party investments among ecosystem partners at the same scale it has done up to this point," Goldman Sachs analyst James Schneider said in a note Thursday.

The news of Huang's resignation comes after investors were already concerned about the massive amount of debt being taken on to fund AI infrastructure.

Tech bond yields have risen and spreads have widened on credit default swaps, most notably in lower-rated names. Credit default swaps are contracts in which investors pay for protection in case the borrower can't repay its debt. Wider spreads indicate investors view the bonds as riskier.

On Friday, the yield on Nvidia's 4.5% bond due in 2031 sat at 5.717%, nearly 5% higher week to date. Bond yields move inversely to prices.

Tech stocks slumped Friday with the Nasdaq 100 closing down 1.2% as markets continued to digest the Nvidia news. Yields on hyperscaler bonds ticked slightly higher on Friday, signaling the broader concern about AI debt lingers.

It's the smaller AI companies that could ultimately see an impact if Nvidia makes any changes to its AI financing. The company had $36 billion in off-balance-sheet AI cloud agreements, or backstops, for neoclouds, according to its last quarterly financial filing in July.

Neoclouds CoreWeave, Nebius and IREN are all in Nvidia's portfolio. Their shares were down sharply Thursday.

CoreWeave, which has become the poster child for AI debt fears, saw its bond yields retreat after its quarterly earnings on Tuesday eased investor concerns. The yield on its 9.75% bond due in 2031 was 14.79% on Friday after climbing to 16.7% last week. The spread on its five-year CDS also dropped more than 17% week to date, although it remained above 1,000 — which is generally considered a sign of distress.

It remains unclear how Nvidia's support for those companies may change, said CreditSights analyst Andy Li.

"We don't know what the ultimate strategy for Nvidia is going to be coming out the other side," he said.

"However, I think directionally, just given the fact that Jensen was so crucial in selling the Nvidia story and being a very aggressive deal maker, it's likely that a lot of this creative deal-making and circular financing and equity and credit support is going to moderate," he added.

CoreWeave CEO Michael Intrator told CNBC Wednesday, before Huang's departure, that Nvidia "is not one person."

"There are thousands of people over there that interface with thousands of people at my company every day. They integrate on the technology. They integrate on the physical infrastructure. They integrate on the networking," he said in an interview with "Squawk on the Street." "They have been a great partner for us for years. They will continue to be a great partner for us."

Bob Lang, founder and chief strategist at Explosive Options, doesn't see any big changes in terms of Nvidia's relevance or its ability to finance for now. As CFO, Kress was involved in the financing deals, and the search for a permanent CEO is going to take some time, he noted.

The real issue is just how much money the company will want to lend for AI financing, rather than, say using its hundreds of billions in free cash flow for other purposes, like share buybacks, capex, or acquisitions.

"Big companies like Nvidia and Meta, they're holding all the cards," he said. "When they decide that the game is over, that's it — it's going to be curtains for some of these smaller companies."

— CNBC'S Kif Leswing and Isabel O'Brien contributed reporting.

<a href="https://www.fiercehealthcare.com/ai-and-machine-learning/dyania-health-nvidia-cleveland-clinic" hreflang="en">Dyania Health, Nvidia team up to bring clinical reasoning AI inside hospital networks</a>

📅 2026-11-13  |  Category: Technology  |  Read Source →
Dyania Health, Nvidia team up to bring clinical reasoning AI inside hospital networks" style="max-width:100%; height:auto; border-radius:8px;" loading="lazy">

Dyania Health is partnering with Nvidia to run its Synapsis AI clinical reasoning platform inside hospitals’ IT systems, enabling large-scale analysis without patient data leaving their networks.

The startup's Synapsis AI reads a patient's full medical record, including clinical notes, imaging and operative reports, labs and other largely unstructured information, and answers clinical questions while pointing back to supporting evidence in the chart. Dyania Health goes beyond summarizing medical records; it uses AI to convert messy, unstructured clinical records into usable datasets and insights.

Nvidia provides the computing infrastructure needed to perform that analysis across potentially entire patient populations behind the hospital firewall, without transferring patient records outside the health system, according to the company.

Dyania brings the clinical reasoning technology and implementation expertise, while Nvidia brings the accelerated computing platform and the software that lets it run securely and efficiently on-premises, Eirini Schlosser, founder and CEO of Dyania Health, told Fierce Healthcare.

Through this collaboration with Nvidia, Dyania's Synapsis AI could help health systems turn large volumes of unstructured clinical data into actionable insights at a scale that would be impractical with manual chart review, while keeping patient data inside the hospital’s own infrastructure, Schlosser said.

Health systems have vast amounts of valuable clinical information locked in unstructured medical records, but manually reviewing those records makes it difficult to use that data at scale for research, registries and predictive models. Synapsis AI aims to remove that bottleneck by analyzing patients’ records longitudinally, determining what happened and when, and identifying the clinical evidence supporting those conclusions, according to the company, which launched out of stealth two years ago.

Frontier models are becoming extraordinarily capable, but the architectures, training data sets, as well as logic are not built to perform clinical reasoning in a real-world healthcare system environment, Schlosser noted.

Dyania's Synapsis AI combines specialized models, a clinician-annotated clinical knowledge base, evidence tracing and hospital-specific implementation. Dyania says it has invested more than 25,000 physician hours annotating medical cases so that Synapsis AI can perform clinical reasoning. This specialized approach is better suited to complex clinical reasoning than a single general-purpose AI model, Schlosser asserted.

"Every patient's story is spread across years of notes, reports and results, and for the first time we can reason across all of it at once, the way a specialist does, for every patient in a health system rather than one chart at a time,” Schlosser said.

Synapsis AI is built on the Nvidia AI enterprise software stack end to end. Dyania trains its proprietary clinical models with the Nvidia NeMo framework for model training and reinforcement learning. Inside the health system, Synapsis AI runs on Nvidia TensorRT and TensorRT-LLM on the hospital's own accelerated computing infrastructure, so inference stays inside the hospital's private network.

"Synapsis AI sits within the health system firewall and is small enough to run inference on local clusters of GPU computing. It does not need to 'speak to the internet' or interact with cloud or frontier models. This provides immense benefits to the healthcare systems for both the comparable cost of tokenomics they would be paying for the frontier models in the cloud as well as for cybersecurity and data privacy of sensitive patient data," Schlosser said. "Hospitals can apply that capability to their patient histories under their own data governance, without sending those records to an external AI service."

Hospitals can use their own historical patient data to determine which treatments work for which patients, identify care gaps and ultimately recommend the next appropriate action, according to Schlosser.

Under the collaboration, the companies will work to bring Synapsis AI on Nvidia infrastructure to health systems in the U.S. and internationally, publish joint case studies and integrate Synapsis AI with Nvidia's healthcare software stack. The companies are exploring additional Nvidia technologies to secure AI processing, handle multiple clinical workloads at once and scale computing capacity, with the goal of moving from batch processing toward near-real-time clinical insights at the point of care.

"Health systems need AI they can trust, integrate into their workflows and operate efficiently. That means connecting information across clinical systems, validating performance for the patients they serve, protecting sensitive data and making results useful within the tools clinicians already use," Chelsea Sumner, Nvidia's U.S. healthcare AI startups ecosystem lead, told Fierce Healthcare.

"Dyania’s approach addresses part of that challenge by running inside the hospital’s own environment and linking findings to evidence in the patient record. Scaling also requires clinicians, technology teams and hospital leaders to work together from the start, with clear responsibility for reviewing results and monitoring performance. Success should be measured by whether AI helps teams find patients who need attention, make better-informed decisions and spend more time delivering care," Sumner said.

Cleveland Clinic used Dyania Health’s Synapsis AI, running on Nvidia infrastructure, to analyze up to 16 years of records from 7,812 aortic valve replacement patients. The study addressed a central concern for patients: How long will the replacement valve last, and will another procedure be needed?

Researchers reviewed nearly 8,000 patient records between 2005 and 2021, mostly narrative notes and echocardiogram reports that registries can struggle to capture.

"Understanding how a replacement heart valve performs means following a patient across years of care, connecting the original operative report with subsequent progress notes, hospitalizations, echocardiograms, other medical conditions and later interventions. Much of that information is buried in narrative records that researchers would otherwise need to review manually," Schlosser noted.

The AI extracted information from narrative clinical records and answered 88 questions per patient about their valves, health conditions and subsequent care. Each answer linked to supporting evidence in the chart, he noted.

Researchers used that dataset to build a predictive model of valve deterioration and the risk of another intervention. The model estimates valve deterioration and repeat-procedure risk at three, five and 10 years post-procedure, with estimates that update as new medical information about the patient becomes available.

"Historically, this would have required human manual abstraction, and for 7,812 patients, it would be humanly impossible to read and abstract features on an ongoing basis at the rate at which medical records are changing. Additionally, humans reading a medical record can often miss information if they skim through it," Schlosser said.

The tool is used to help inform care but requires external validation from clinicians.

"Using technology to bring together and analyze information that can help us predict the duration of implanted heart valves is a promising step towards enhanced outcomes and more personalized care for patients," said Lars G. Svensson, M.D., Ph.D., chief of the Heart, Vascular and Thoracic Institute at Cleveland Clinic, in a statement.

The health system began working with Dyania Health a year ago to use its AI platform for clinical trial recruitment.

Synapsis AI made it possible for the first time to comprehensively analyze nearly two decades of patient data, Schlosser asserted. "What was even more groundbreaking was the ability to go from raw data in unstructured form to predictive risk models in one fell swoop. This enables precision care at scale and empowers physicians with stronger sets of information backing their clinical decisions about any given patient, including questions like 'when should the patient have their next echo?' or 'when will the patient likely need a reintervention?'" Schlosser said.

The Cleveland Clinic and Dyania Health collaboration reflects Nvidia's broader focus to provide healthcare and life sciences innovators with the computing platform and AI tools to advance research and help care teams better understand patients’ needs, Sumner said.

The heart valve study shows how Synapsis AI could help health systems use their own patient data to determine which treatments work best for which patients and improve predictive models over time, ultimately supporting more personalized care recommendations, according to Dyania Health.

"Nvidia's infrastructure enables us to handle more work concurrently and use resources more efficiently. That could allow hospitals to examine larger populations, ask more detailed questions and revisit analyses more frequently. The longer-term opportunity is to move from periodic batches of records toward insights available closer to the moment a clinician needs them," Schlosser said.

"We can do that within the health system’s own environment, keeping patient records behind its firewall. We are also evaluating capabilities for distributed inference, workload isolation and protection of data during computation. Computing power alone does not make a clinical conclusion correct; it allows a carefully developed clinical system to work at greater scale and speed," he said.

Sumner asserts that healthcare organizations are just scratching the surface on the potential for AI to uncover clinically useful information buried in longitudinal patient records.

"Connecting a physician’s notes with earlier test results and treatment history could help identify patients who need follow-up, match people with clinical trials and give researchers a clearer understanding of how treatments perform over time," she said. "The Cleveland Clinic heart valve study is a concrete example. AI helped researchers assemble a detailed view of patients’ care to study how replacement valves deteriorate. The opportunity is to turn that knowledge into more personalized monitoring and better-informed care decisions. Clinicians need to be able to review the supporting evidence, validate the findings and decide what they mean for each patient."

Nvidia stock suffers longest weekly losing streak since 2012 as market value sinks by $1.7 trillion

📅 2026-11-13  |  Category: Technology  |  Read Source →

Nvidia investors turned bearish before this week's Jensen Huang saga. But the selling on Wall Street accelerated in the past few days, sending the stock to its sixth straight weekly drop, the longest losing streak since 2012.

The chip giant, which spent most of the year as the world's most valuable company, has lost 30% of its value during losing streak. That's a drop of roughly $1.7 trillion in market cap, and it fell below Apple in the process.

Huang, who co-founded Nvidia and led it for 33 years, resigned on Thursday after two separate extramarital affairs — one with an alleged Chinese spy and the other with an employee — were made public. The board named finance chief Colette Kress as interim CEO while it conducts a search for a full-time successor.

Nvidia shares fell 13% this week, the most since April 2025. News of the first reported affair hit the front pages over the weekend, when Huang sent a letter to employees apologizing for being "unfaithful to my wife." The board convened late Wednesday after The New York Times reported on the other affair, this one with the company's vice president of health care.

By early Thursday morning, Huang was out, capping a stunning fall for the Nvidia co-founder, who had emerged as one of President Donald Trump's top allies in the corporate world.

"With the unfortunate departure of CEO Jensen Huang we expect a challenging transition for NVIDIA over the next few months," Gil Luria, an analyst at D.A. Davidson, wrote in a report on Thursday. Luria lowered his price target to $200 from $300, but maintained his buy rating. "We believe the market has appropriately adjusted for this transition," he wrote.

Last week, prior to Huang's departure, Nvidia shares dropped about 9%. Much of the decline came after the midterm elections, which resulted in sweeping victories for Democrats and the passage of dozens of ballot measures that could slow the artificial intelligence buildout.

In the weeks before the election, Nvidia's stock was sliding alongside the rest of the AI trade on concerns that rising interest rates would punish debt-heavy companies. While Nvidia is wildly profitable, big customers like neoclouds are reliant on the debt markets.

Heading into next week, the pressure is on Kress. Nvidia is scheduled to report quarterly results on Tuesday. Analysts are projecting 91% year-over-year revenue growth to $108.9 billion, according to LSEG. That's up 18-fold from the same quarter in 2022, just before OpenAI launched ChatGPT and kicked off the generative AI era.

Analysts at Oppenheimer wrote in a report on Thursday that, even though they see the company reporting solid earnings, "we expect fundamentals to take a backseat near term."

"The departure of Mr. Huang could, in our view, translate to a lingering share overhang," they wrote.
